speechtext:
I shall only occupy the time of the House for a few minutes, and in those few minutes I shall give almost exclusive attention to the amendment to the amendment which was tabled last evening. Indeed, I would not have intervened, so far as I know my own mind or intentions, in the debate, but for the tabling of that amendment. Before saying a few words about it, however, I should like to be permitted to offer my sincere congratulations to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition for the words which he spoke in regard to the peaceful relations which have .existed so long between this country and The United States of America, words which received emphatic endorsement by the First Minister of the Crown. I thank my hon. friend the leader of the opposition very sincerely for those words, because they afford to every one in Canada evidence that when, as may probably happen in the course of what I think will be some time, he comes to occupy the position of the First Minister, we shall have a man who has a due sense of the weighty responsibility of Canada in being an important factor ip maintaining the peace of the world.
Now, I should like also, before turning to look for a few minutes at this amendment, to say that I, as one who supported the policy of my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on the
navy question last year, have derived a very considerable confirmation of the wisdom of my position from what I venture to describe as the universal endorsation of that policy in the old country. That feeling is perhaps very natural to me, but I think it ought to be shared by all Canadians because we all realize that in the old country you have, on both sides of politics, men with very keen insight into politics, men who have centuries of training at their back, and when you have a policy carried out by the Canadian government, endorsed by both sides of politics in the old country, it affords, I think, presumptive evidence of the wisdom of that policy. At all events it gives me the very greatest satisfaction. When the navy debate was going on last year we had this endorsation coming from so strong a unionist organ as the ' Morning Post ' in unequivocal terms. I need not mention the liberal endorsation of the policy. It was impossible that the Liberal party and the Liberal press of Great Britain should not. endorse that policy, founded, as it is, upon Canadian autonomy, and based upon perfect freedom within the great commonwealth of nations constituting the British Empire-such an empire as has never been seen before. But, I noticed that so strong an imperialist as Sir George Doughty visited the city of Edmonton this year and that he was interviewed, as all prominent Britishers coming to this country are interviewed at the present time. Amongst other* things he was interviewed upon the opinion of the old country with regard to the naval policy of the Liberal government. Sir George Doughty is an imperialist of the imperialists, he is a very strong member of the Liberal Unionist party at home and what had. he to say about the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier?
Sir Wilfrid Laurier

He said:
-has done a great service to Canada and to the empire in establishing the Canadian navy. You are a nation, and as such should equip yourselves for the duty of defence. I think it would have been a mistake to make a contribution to the British navy, either in money or ships. As your Canadian navy grows you will be training your own men for the sea and creating the spirit of naval enterprise. The people will develop the sense of nationality; they will develop the spirit which has made the British navy what it is, and the spirit of the nation is worth more than ten warships.
This is a remarkable piece of testimony from a prominent man in the Unionist party in Great Britain to the wisdom of the navy policy of the right hon. gentleman and his government. I follow, as carefully as I know how, opinion in the old country. I have the opportunity of reading its papers, I meet visitors from there and I have not

seen any contrary opinion that was worthy of attention.
Now, I turn to look for a few minutes at the amendment which is the subject of debate at the present moment. I should like to say in the first place that the amendment appears to me to be a very great triumph for the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I ventured to describe the amendment of the leader of the opposition last session as an omnibus amendment. I described it as an omnibus amendment with eompai'tments, but the triumph of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier is in this, that while he was in solitary confinement at that time in his own compartment, he has developed a strength which would never have been suspected in a man of a so commonly lamb-like disposition, though he departed very strongly from that description of him the other day. He has broken down all the other compartments, has captured the entire omnibus and has even, as far as I can see, invaded the driver's seat. He is not just trying to depose his leader, but he has certainly deposed the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and, as far as I can see, he seriously contemplates putting Bour-assa in his place. This is surely not exaggerated language. If my hon. friends of the opposition think it is I should like to address to them one question. What has become of the proposal to give a contribution to Britain in their attitude on this question? Where are the Dreadnoughts under the present proposition? If they will keep on debating the naval policy we must debate it. They thought the German war scare was imminent twelve months ago. Well, it ought to be more imminent now. What has become of the German scare which was the cause of their resolution of last year? I take it that the elimination of the proposal to give money immediately to Great Britain is tantamount to a confession that their attitude of twelve months ago was entirely wrong and that the case that they built up last year upon the German war-scare falls to the ground, and I am sure that the country will consider it just as likely that the case they put up at the present time will have fallen to the ground twelve months hence. But what is the amendment which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition tabled last evening?
It is a; protestation coupled with a doubt. I agree with my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) that the protestation is not at all necessary, and least of all should it be necessary on the part of the leader of the opposition. But I take it that the protestation was put in to satisfy the aspirations of such as my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes). I can imagine the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) reminding his leader that he had many a time advocated full partnership union within the empire, and Mr. M. CLARK.
that no motion dealing with foreign or imperial politics could possibly .be complete without a protestation of loyalty. And then, when the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) was getting his way in that respect the member for Jacques Cartier comes on the scene and he infuses his doubt. Now, there can be no exception taken to the protestation. But, since I have come to this country nine years ago, and as I have moved among the Canadian people I have discovered in them a loyalty which almost exceeds the loyalty of the strongest imperialist at home. I do not think that any one who knows the Canadian people can have any doubt of their loyalty, or can see the necessity for expressing it in words. No man is continually professing his extreme attachment to his parents, or if he does we begin to have some doubts about his sincerity. We are loyal in Canada; of course we are loyal; we are loyal in every portion of the British Empire; we are loyal because we are free. What is it that we are loyal to? The resolution asks us to express our loyalty to the Crown of Britain. Yes, but the Crown is an emblem of something, and what is it that the Crown is an emblem of? It is the emblem of an empire such as the world has never seen. What is the cement which binds the British Empire together? It is not community of language for" the Sikhs of India speak a different language from the natives of New Zealand; it is not community of religions because the British flag floats over all religions. What is the cement that binds us of the British Empire together and makes us loyal? Sir, it is the knowledge in the hearts and the minds of every one of us that wherever the British flag flies, wherever the British Empire holds sway you have a guarantee that there will be bestowed upon the sons of men the greatest freedom combined with the greatest love for law and order that the world has ever seen. And, Sir, it is because my right hon. friend has embodied such a belief, and such a principle in his naval policy that I am an enthusiastic supporter of that policy. May I say that I regret that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) should rise in his place and express the opinion that conscription could possibly be resorted to in Canada. Upon what facts in history does he rely for that assertion? I wonder he had not the chivalry of his race to remember that while every other nation in Europe is under more or less autocratic government-except the republic of France-they have conscription, in these two little islands sticking out into the German ocean which constitute the island heart of our empire, there is no conscription? What Britain has done by land or sea she has done by the exercise of that freedom which is the glory of her empire. I am, of course, in agreement with

the expression of loyalty in the resolution, but what bothers me is that the leader of the opposition should have attached to his resolution a doubt that the people of Canada are not ready to assume the logical outcome of the unanimous resolution of this House passed the session before last.
I should like to go a step further in the examination of this amendment and I would ask the leader of the opposition what would happen if the amendment is carried. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) disclaimed any idea that a referendum would be the outcome and I agree with him in his interpretation of the resolution. The only outcome of the carrying of the resolution would be the precipitation of a general election, and I want to ask my hon. friend who occupies the responsible position of leader of the opposition if he thinks it would tend to build up the empire or the Canadian nation that a general election should be precipitated on this delicate question of the foreign policy of the empire, and the imperial connection. In such a general election would the opposition support the building of a Canadian navy? You would have this question thrown into the turmoil of public meetings from the Atlantic to the Pacific ; you would have a discussion throughout the west where you have a large and varied population, whom, I take it to be the duty of every man who has the instincts of statesmanship to train up to be sound Canadians ; you would have these people brought face to face at once with a question of the utmost delicacy, and I ask the leader of the apposition in all sincerity if such a thing would commend itself to his mature deliberation in the months and years that are to come. If such an election were precipitated would honourable gentlemen opposite support the proposal to build a Canadian navy? I should like an answer to that question by some hon. gentleman who follows me. If they would support the building of a Canadian navy then there is no need of an election and we had better go on with the business of the country. But, if they would not support the building of a Canadian navy, what then becomes of all their protestations of loyalty? Now, suppose they carried the election and they carried out the policy indicated in the amendment, they would simply be going around the country saying to the people that they wanted a mandate from them, not knowing exactly what the mandate was about. I suppose if they carried the election it would at any rate be taken as a vote against the government and against its naval policy. Then, we should have the wonderful spectacle of a party which has always boasted of imperial connection and its fondness for the empire, and which boasts it in the preliminary words of this very amendment, telling the ' Niobe ' and tae ' Rainbow ' solemnly : You must go back across the Atlantic ; we cannot build any Canadian navy at present. And then, my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) would, I presume, rush to the seashore as lie has done before when the empire was in danger, and he would call out : Come back ' Niobe ' come back ' Rainbow ', I am going to propose once more my resolution in favour of a full partnership union in the empire. Mr. Speaker, I do not think this amendment-and this is my chief objection to it-I do not think it sizes up the greatness of the future destiny of Canada and of the Canadian people. If my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (who is going to the west next year where I am perfectly sure he will get a most hearty welcome)- will permit me, I shall read to him a paragraph from the Saturday ' News ' of Edmonton, an independent paper, which embodies better than I can in my own language what I conceive to be the future greatness and destiny of the Canadian people.
Indeed it begins to look as if Canada were destined to be one of the great ' carrying ' nations of the world. Already our ocean-going shipping compares favourably with that of the United States in spite of the disparity in our population. The tremendous growth in Canadian shipping has helped immensely to keep the British flag in the proud position of flying on more and greater ships than all the other nations of the world put together. Fifty years ago, the British flag floated over 54 per cent of the world's shipping; to-day it floats over 59 per cent. And Canada has helped in that. The Canadian Pacific railway alone has sixty-five ocean and lake vessels, and a traveller may go from Liverpool to Yokohama without leaving a Canadian Pacific railway conveyance'.
If Canada continues her success in the maritime trade, it will have a profound effect on her national life. When Canadian ships are afloat on every ocean, and Canadian seamen are in every foreign port, we shall begin to know something of international law and international responsibility. We shall look upon the policing of the seas in a different way, and shall become more deeply interested in the questions on which international peace depend. We shall have problems much broader than the price of lumber and wheat or the rate of duty on barbed wire and agricultural implements. International Itravel broadens the individual; international trade expands the horizon of the nation.
I am bound to say that I think my hon. friend owes me a debt of gratitude for drawing his attention to that paragraph in a paper published in the great west because it gives him an idea of the largeness of view, the breadth and expansion of the outlook, of the people he is going to visit next year, and I can assure him that he

will have to size up to that view if he expects to carry the west for his party. I do not think he quite sizes up to it when he tables an amendment such as that which we are considering to-day. I do not think he will build up an empire or a nation, or even the fortunes of his party, with an amendment characterized by what I cannot help calling benevolent ineptitude. My hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) said something about a recent visit to the west. He gives a very different account of the reception of the Prime Minister from that which I should have been disposed to give, who took part in it. I attended in the city of Calgary one of several meetings during that tour. Calgary, I am aware, is represented in this House by a Conservative member, and the reception which the Prime Minister got in Calgary is all the more remarkable on that account. I count the member for Calgary amongst my personal friends, and I hare my doubts whether, if the party had a man of less personal charm to represent them, they.would be able to keep the city of Calgary for the Conservative party. 'Well, I attended in that city one of the most remarkable meetings I have attended in my life, a meeting at which there were
10,000	people. A great number of them must have been Conservatives, and I want to assure this House that when the right hon. the Prime Minister, in language of evident sincerity, told the audience that next to his belief in his religion, was his! belief in Canada, sitting on the platform as I was permitted to do, I felt there and then that we have a man who sizes up to the responsibilities of his position, and to the aspirations and the future destinies of this country. That is the reason why, if our hon. friends opposite carried their amendment, I have not the slightest doubt in my own mind what would be the result of an appeal to the people of western Canada at the present time on this, or any other of the great issues which have been raised in the address. Because I think the policy of the Prime Minister, embodying as it does the highest staesmanship, the greatest political wisdom, that statesmanship and wisdom being in accordance with what has been the treatment of the colonies, as they were at one time called, by the mother country for a great many years past-a policy endorsed for many years by both parties in the old country-it is because of that I will vote with the utmost confidence against the amendment proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to hear the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), who has just sat down, make a speech in this House. For one Mr. CLARK.	.
thing, he uses very forcible diction; for another, he has what we all on this side of the House recognize as very robust patriotism. I fear, however, that while his powers of sarcasm are still as fresh and strong as ever, his powers of logic have been sadly astray in the address he has given us. The hon. member argues that the only way in which the people of Canada can really express their loyalty to the empire is by building a Canadian navy according to the government's programme, while another member on that side of the House, the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Turcotte) argued that the building of this very same navy was the necessary and logical step towards independence. I shall have to leave it to my hon. friend from Red Deer and to the hon. member for Nicolet to reconcile two such widely divergent opinions on the particular question at issue. The hon. member for Red Deer suggests that the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition is a dangerous amendment, which, if it carried, would have certain disastrous consequences. Of course, we are not so sanguine as to believe that the government will readily let any of our motions or suggestions carry with the majority they have and with their usual practice; but why is my hon. friend so afraid of the disastrous consequences of this amendment, if it carried? Because, he says, we shall have a general election, in the first place. That would be bad; and it seems to me that I read between the lines that there was fear of the people in the hearts of hon. gentlemen opposite if an election took place, and that the hon. member for Red Deer was put up partly to explain the attitude of members voting against this amendment and provide them with arguments with their constituents. If his line of argument is true with regard to this amendment, that if we had a general appeal to the country at this particular time it would upset the programme of the government, and show to the country at large and the empire a divided House in regard to this programme of naval construction, he provides the very answer I would give him, that it was ours and his bound en duty to vote for an appeal to the country when that policy was formulated last year. We cannot get away from that and with that particular phase of this whole matter I hope to deal a little later on.
After the too brief recess of the past summer, we find ourselves once more in this,
I would almost say stuffy chamber, theoretically to transact the nation's business and in reality, as far as we have gone in this debate, to discuss in detail the late election in Quebec and to thresh out a great deal of old straw. In this respect as 1 in some other respects I would point out I that the speech of the Minister of Marine

and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), was a performance little calculated to uphold the prestige and dignity which should accompany the utterances of a minister of the Crown in this House. I shall join with other members of this House in congratulating the mover of the address on his speech and while it is true that we on this side necessarily cannot approve of the matter of that sneech we can, I think, and do heartily approve of its manner, and I also have to thank him for setting so signal an example /of 'brevity which certainly every one of us here might well emulate.
Others beside myself would probably not have taken part in this debate if it had not been for the amendments referred to by the last speaker which are now before the House. The nature of the amendments and some of the arguments used in connection with the naval questions must form my excuse for speaking, for I feel I cannot give a silent vote on the amendment. Before dealing with this question, however, the House will, I trust, pardon a word or two in reference to another matter which has already been touched on in this debate, I refer to the Prime Minister's tour of the west. That tour was, I think, an excellent thing for the Prime Minister. I think it was also an excellent _thing for the country and if I may be pardoned for looking at its strictly political aspect I may say it was not at all a bad thing for the members on this side of the House. When we take into consideration the vastness of this country, the rapidity of its western development especially and the complexity of its problems, I am sure that every member of the House will agree that public men who are deputed by the people to assume the burden and responsibility of administering the affairs of the country would be in a vastly better position, they would be vastly better equipped for that task if they familiarized themselves by first hand knowledge with the country's condition and with special reference to my fellow citizens in Quebec, I would like to express the belief that a personal visit to the west of the leading men of the province of Quebec, with a sympathetic study of the varied and energetic life of the west, would be an invaluable help in the establishment of better relations between Quebec and the English speaking provinces^ of the Dominion. It would, I believe, give them a better conception of the real solidarity of the Canadian people and I believe it would tend to a quicker and happier solution of many of the vexed problems that come before this House. I might echo the suggestion of a very prominent statesman in Great Britain who said that he believed it would be a good thing for parliament to vote supplies for a year, to lock up the House, and send all the members for a trip around the whole length and breadth
of their country, and when it was argued that the country might go to the dogs meanwhile, he suggested it would be perfectly well taken care of by the permanent heads of departments. Something of the same kind might happen here with some advantage to the government; it even might save them from some egregious blunders.	.
Of course the tour was not without its humorous side. On this side of the House it is difficult for us to repress a smile as one imagines the fiery language with which such a tour would have been greeted by my right hon. friend and the leader of his party in the Senate, if it had been conducted by the Conservative party in the old days. Had such a semi-royal procession then wended its way through the country with the same prearranged meetings-of tomtoms, with the advance agents whom we all met every now and then through the west, how they would have fulminated against the pride of luxury of all these undemocratic exhibitions. The Prime Minister will perhaps say that times have changed to a large extent. Personally, I am inclined to think that this is becoming a good deal of a one-man government; if there were any doubt about that I think we need only note how, when our friends opposite are hard pushed, put on the line of last defence, they always indulge in a brilliant eulogy of the Prime Minister who is regarded as the chief and perhaps the only asset of the party. If that is so, perhaps, it is necessary that there should _ be some splendour of pageantry in the Prime Minister's visit to the west. I do not cavil at that.
When the Prime Minister reached Vancouver, he announced at his meeting that his trip was of a non-political character and it was made not so much with the idea of discussing politics as to ascertain the resources of the country and to endeavour in a sympathetic way to see what its great needs were. The trip would have had a better result to the Prime Minister and his government if he had faithfully complied with this programme, which he laid down for himself. When, as on some occasions on which I had the honour of meeting him, he did comply, he will agree with me that he found a warm welcome and a warm response from our people; they were broadminded in their welcome of the first citizen of Canada, although they may have dissented and dissented heartily from his various policies. But when he, himself, and especially his colleagues took upon themselves to deliver campaign speeches of the conventional and narrowest type, I can say-and I am speaking more particularly of my own province-that they not only vastly underrated the intelligence of their audiences, but they offended the canons of I the best taste and I am absolutely certain

that _ they shattered any hopes of gaining political headway in British Columbia.
My right hon. friend twitted me good-humouredly in Nelson with trying to put him out of his job. I have some little_ aspirations in that direction yet, and I might even venture the remark that my hon. friend was never less secure in that job than at the present time.
Reference was made by the hon. the leader of the opposition to a question that affects the people of British Columbia. He had been accused, he said, by the Prime Minister of bribing British Columbia because he had volunteered that a certain large question affecting that province should be submitted to an impartial arbitration board if and when he came into power, and the Prime Minister was asked, in reply, that if this was bribery what was the unblushing offer of public works in every constituency the Prime Minister visited?
I regret that the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) is not here in order that I may say to his face what I have to say. The Minister of Inland Revenue at one of these meetings of the government party in my own riding touched this particular question, and when the Minister of Inland Revenue touches any prominent British Columbia question he usually displays a marvellous and fatal facility for blundering. He attempted, on this occasion, on August 25, in the city of Vernon, to deal with the question of better terms, a cry which he regretted to say was likely to spring up again, and he added-and here I am quoting from the notes I took of his words:-
I say that the government by giving assistance to railways, by building post offices and by giving experimental farms

I may interject that if the Minister of Agriculture is going to give these farms he had better give them quickly-
-this is a far better sort of better terms than by giving money to the McBride government.
Let me ask the Minister of Inland Revenue or the Prime Minister, who heard these words, which I can only describe as the most fatuous of utterances, whether they would now endorse them and what they mean? These people, who have overwhelmingly supported Mr. McBride and his administration, are regarded as having no intelligence, as having no wrongs to right, and we are told that it would be far better to hand them out sops from the public treasury, carefully administered by supporters of the government, and thus keep them quiet, rather than hand over the money to those whom the people declare emphatically are their trustees. After this amazing declaration the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) expressed the hope that even his friend the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) will yet see Mr. BURRELL.
the errors of his ways and support the present administration. Well, if I ever felt the slightest inclination to support the right hon. gentleman and his government, that inclination would have been effectively suppressed by the character of the speeches delivered by the government party at that particular meeting. If, on these points, or on the naval question, my right hon. friend wishes to test the feeling of the country, let him open a constituency out there, because, as I understand, this is a closed season for senatorships in the province of Quebec. And in order to open a constituency in British Columbia I would suggest to the right hon. gentleman that he should re-translate our friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) to the Senate. No doubt the peaceful atmosphere of that chamber would be more suitable to him and bring him more happiness. If the Prime Minister will do this he will find out very effectively what the western people really think of him and his administration.
The right hon. gentleman said some very pleasant things about our section of the country. After a very nice description of the strong feeling which Manitoba had aroused in him and a still more flattering description of the attractions he found in Saskatchewan -and the charms and beauties of Alberta, he remarked that the beauties and the charms of British Columbia had irresistibly appealed to his feelings. To such an extent did they appeal to him that if he were not unfortunately kept in the east by the cares and responsibilities of office, he would certainly choose Vernon as a place of residence. I might say that the prospect of his retaining office for many years seem to me rather dubious at present, and I would express the hope that when the time comes when he shall have to retire he will take up his residence in Vernon, and, perhaps, then, to use the Minister of Inland Revenue's words, he will be able to see the error of his ways and support my hon. friend (Mr. Borden), and he can then add to his other courtesies by marking his ballot for the Conservative candidate. As it is six o'clock I move that the debate do now adjourn.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.
Monday, November 28, 1910.
